title: Low Floor High Ceiling Maths Tasks Are Not the Solution
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman critically examines the 'low floor, high ceiling' task concept — the idea that open, accessible tasks through which students of all levels can engage differently solve the differentiation problem in mixed-ability maths classrooms. Ashman, a longtime critic of differentiation as commonly practiced, acknowledges the appeal: if one task can serve all students, the impossible workload of planning multiple differentiated tasks disappears. But he argues that the appeal is largely illusory. Low floor, high ceiling tasks may get all students 'into' a task, but they do not reliably ensure that all students are learning what they most need to learn at the right level of challenge; high-attaining students often coast on surface engagement while lower-attaining students struggle with the floor entry that is still too high for them. Ashman's alternative leans on the evidence for explicit instruction and direct teaching: giving students the knowledge and skills they need before encountering a task, rather than hoping task design will scaffold the gap. The article is characteristic of Ashman's evidence-based, skeptical approach to progressive maths pedagogy.
points: Low floor, high ceiling tasks solve the planning problem (one task for all students) while not reliably solving the learning problem (ensuring all students are appropriately challenged and learning what they need).

The theoretical appeal of accessible-to-all task design collapses in practice: the 'low floor' may still be too high for students without the foundational knowledge the task assumes, while the 'high ceiling' rarely produces the depth of understanding that structured practice does.

Ashman's implicit alternative — direct instruction that builds knowledge before tasks — represents a fundamentally different theory of what tasks are for: not discovery vehicles but consolidation and application opportunities for knowledge already taught.

The article's strongest evidence-based challenge is to the differentiation assumption itself: if all students can benefit from the same high-quality direct instruction, the premise that they need differently designed tasks may be wrong.

For maths teachers and curriculum designers, the practical implication is that effort spent on clever task design may be better spent on sequencing what knowledge students need before they encounter the task.

I am a long-term sceptic of ‘differentiation’ or ‘differentiated instruction’.
That would seem to fix the problem of planning many different tasks, while also allowing for differentiation. Students could be grouped within the class and tackle the task differently.

This is because problem solving taxes mental resources to the extent that there is often no attention left over to notice patterns. Instead, if we want students to learn mathematics, a planned, sequenced approach where concepts are explicitly introduced would seem to be a better bet [ ].
I am therefore not sure exactly what mathematics this is targeting. The prompt mentions students ‘may construct models using dynamic geometric software and apply trigonometry’.

Unfortunately, I can see it keeping students busy for an extended period of time and I worry that may be the attraction. What is clear is that despite the framing, these tasks are cover for a form of inquiry learning.

This is a highly significant constraint and is essentially the same constraint as a low floor/threshold. Kapur managed this constraint in some of his work by focusing on standard deviation and asking which baseball player was the most consistent.

Low floor high ceiling tasks therefore are a form of inquiry learning, but they are an impoverished form even of inquiry learning. Worse, they are designed to generate busywork and activity that looks like students are doing mathematics when they are not learning anything much at all.
